pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny, slender pale-yellow to brown insects hiding down in the leaf folds, leaving silvery or whitish streaks and flecks on the green blades. Bad infestations make the foliage look bleached and papery.
pests.cause_beginner: Thrips are minute sap-sucking insects, common on onion-family plants, that rasp the leaves and are worst in hot, dry weather. Chives usually shrug them off, but a heavy year can mark the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hose the plants down to knock thrips off, shear a badly streaked clump to the base so it regrows clean, and use insecticidal soap on the leaves if needed. Rinse cut leaves before use.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered in hot spells, welcome helpful insects like lacewings and pirate bugs, and cut a marked-up clump back to force fresh leaves.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) feeding in the leaf axils and folds, producing silvery-white stippling, streaking, and a bleached, papery look on heavy pressure; they favor hot, dry weather. On chives the damage is usually cosmetic, but a severe year degrades a leaf crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Thrips tabaci, the principal allium thrips, rasps leaf surfaces and feeds on the sap; populations build fast in hot, dry conditions and on stressed plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge with a strong water jet, shear a heavily infested clump to the base to remove the population and force clean regrowth, and spray insecticidal soap or spinosad if warranted; conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings). Keeping plants unstressed and watered blunts outbreaks.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid drought stress, conserve natural enemies, cut back streaked foliage to reset the clump, and avoid siting chives beside heavily thrips-pressured onion or garlic plantings.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.symptoms_beginner: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf where the adult fly fed, then wavy pale mines inside the leaves, with small maggots or brown seed-like pupae tucked into the leaf bases. It shows up in spring and again in fall.
pests.cause_beginner: The allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae tunnel inside onion-family leaves, including chives, and burrow toward the base. It is a newer pest in parts of the eastern United States.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover plants with floating row cover in early spring and again in fall to keep the flies off, cut off and destroy mined leaves, and clean up plant debris.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover during the spring and fall flights, remove mined leaves, and keep the bed clean.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma): lines of white oviposition punctures down the distal leaf, followed by larval mines and brown puparia lodged in leaf sheaths and bulbs. The University of Maryland lists chive (A. schoenoprasum) among its hosts; wounds open the door to secondary bacterial and fungal rots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive allium-specific fly with a spring flight (roughly March into May) and a fall flight (September into October); larvae mine toward the leaf base and bulb, with up to dozens of pupae per plant in severe cases.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover timed to the spring and fall flights, remove and destroy mined foliage, and sanitize crop debris; spinosad or azadirachtin can help where pressure is high. Rotation away from recently infested allium ground reduces carryover.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row-cover through both flight periods, remove infested leaves, sanitize residue, and separate new plantings from pressured allium beds.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth as small white maggots tunnel into the base of the plant and the bulbs below the soil, sometimes rotting the crown. Worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.cause_beginner: Onion maggots are the larvae of a fly that lays eggs at the base of onion-family plants; the maggots eat into the roots and bulbs. Chives are rarely hit hard, but a clump can be damaged.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home-garden spray for maggots already inside a plant, so pull badly affected plants, roots and all, and get rid of them. Keep the flies off with row cover put on at planting, and do not leave old bulbs or culls lying around, since rotting onion material draws the fly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put row cover on at planting, before the flies are out, but not over ground that grew onions or their relatives last year, or you trap the emerging flies under it. Clear away old bulbs and culls, keep fresh manure out of the bed in spring, and give chives a spot away from last year's onion beds.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Onion maggot (Delia antiqua) larvae mining into the basal plate, roots, and bulbs, causing wilting, yellowing, stunting, and crown rot; damage is worst in cool, moist springs and where allium debris accumulates. Established chive clumps are seldom destroyed but can be set back.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia antiqua overwinters as pupae in the soil around last season's alliums; spring flies lay eggs at plant bases and successive generations attack roots and bulbs, favored by cool, wet weather and drawn to rotting organic matter, fresh manure and cull piles.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infested plants with their roots, exclude the flies with row cover sealed at the edges from planting, and clear culls and volunteer alliums, which sustain the population between crops. Rotate off last year's allium ground and keep new plantings away from it, since the pupae overwinter in the soil there. No home-garden insecticide is available for maggots once larvae are in the crown.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Cover from planting on ground that did not carry alliums last year, remove lifted plants and culls in fall to take the pupae out with them, hold spring manure and green manure out of the bed, and rotate: the flies emerge from the soil where alliums grew last season.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, fuzzy gray-violet patches on the leaves in cool, damp weather, with the blades yellowing and collapsing. It spreads fastest in wet, crowded, poorly drained plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like disease of the onion family, favored by cool, humid, wet conditions, that can affect chives along with onions, garlic, and leeks.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow by dividing crowded clumps, water at the base rather than over the leaves, and cut a badly hit clump back so it regrows in drier weather.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space and divide plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid soggy, shaded, crowded spots.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora destructor) producing pale oval patches that turn violet-gray with sporulation under moisture, with leaves paling, yellowing, and collapsing; it is favored by cool (below about 75°F), humid, wet conditions and affects chives among many alliums.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete spread by wind and splashing water and favored by cool, moist weather and long leaf-wetness periods; crowded, poorly drained plantings hold it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Manage culturally: divide crowded clumps and space for airflow, irrigate at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump to regrow under drier conditions. The home garden has no reliable cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open the canopy by dividing, water at the base, site in well-drained sun, and avoid the cool, wet, crowded conditions the pathogen needs.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Bright orange raised spots or streaks (pustules) scattered on the leaves. Heavily rusted blades yellow and dry up. It is more common in wet seasons and on crowded, over-fed plants.
diseases.cause_beginner: Rust is a fungal disease of the onion family, including chives, that shows as orange pustules on the leaves and spreads by airborne spores in damp weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and destroy rusty leaves or shear the clump to the base to regrow clean, thin crowded plantings for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and heavy nitrogen.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room and airflow, water at the base, go easy on nitrogen, and remove rusty foliage promptly.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Allium rust (Puccinia species) forming bright orange to rusty raised pustules on leaves and scapes, with chlorosis and dieback of heavily infected foliage; it is favored by moist conditions, crowding, and lush high-nitrogen growth, and affects chives along with garlic, leeks, and onions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Puccinia rust fungi spread by airborne urediniospores in humid weather; dense stands and excess nitrogen worsen it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Shear infected foliage (a hard cut to the base removes the pustules and regrows clean), divide to open crowded clumps, avoid overhead irrigation and heavy nitrogen, and remove debris. Fungicides are rarely warranted in a home planting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Divide for airflow, moderate nitrogen, irrigate at the soil line, and cut out rust early before it spreads.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellowing, wilting plants whose roots and crown rot, with a fluffy white mold and tiny black specks (like poppy seeds) at the base. Affected plants do not recover, and the disease stays in the soil for many years.
diseases.cause_beginner: White rot is a serious soil fungus of the onion family that rots the roots and crown. Once it is in the soil it lasts a very long time, so keeping it out is the whole game.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure. Remove and destroy affected plants along with the soil around the roots, and do not plant chives, onions, or garlic in that spot again. Never move infected soil or plants to a clean bed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean plants, do not bring in soil from an infected garden, and rotate onion-family plants to fresh ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) causing yellowing, wilting, and a soft rot of roots and crown, with a fluffy white mycelium and abundant tiny black sclerotia at the base; the sclerotia persist in soil for many years, and the disease affects chives with onions, garlic, and leeks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum, a soilborne fungus favored by cool, moist soil; its long-lived sclerotia make an infested site unusable for alliums for a decade or more, so exclusion and sanitation are the only real controls.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue: rogue out affected plants with surrounding soil, avoid spreading infested soil on tools or transplants, and do not replant alliums in the site. Long rotation is the standing management.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean, sclerotia-free stock, quarantine infested ground from alliums, sanitize tools, and never import garden soil of unknown history.

diseases.name: Botrytis (leaf blight and neck rot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small whitish sunken spots on the leaves in cool, wet weather, often with a pale green halo, that can run together and brown out the leaf tips. It is worst where the leaves stay wet for a long time and in crowded plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: Botrytis leaf blight is a fungus of the onion family that spots and blights the leaves when they stay wet for most of a day in cool weather, and crowded, still plantings hold that wetness longest.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut the clump back hard and clear the cut leaves away so it regrows clean, open up crowded plantings for airflow, and water at the base instead of over the leaves so the foliage dries between waterings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space and divide for airflow, water at the soil line at a time of day that lets the leaves dry, and clear out dead foliage at the end of the season.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Botrytis leaf blight (Botrytis squamosa): small white sunken oval spots, 0.06 to 0.25 inch, often with a light green halo, that coalesce into tip dieback and blighted leaves under cool, moist conditions. Leaves need 20 or more hours of wetness for spots to form, and poor air circulation in a crowded stand favors it. It is documented on onion, and chives are a related host.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis squamosa, favored by cool, wet weather and dense canopies; its spores are airborne, and they infect only where leaf wetness lasts 20 hours or more. It overwinters as sclerotia on infected leaves, culls and debris, which persist in the soil for months to years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Shear the clump and remove the cut foliage rather than leaving it in the bed, since sclerotia form on infected leaves; divide to open the stand so leaves dry, water at the soil line and time it so foliage dries before night, and clear dead foliage and debris at the end of the season. Fungicides are seldom warranted on a home chive planting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Divide for airflow, water at the base and time it for leaf drying, keep new plantings off ground that carried diseased alliums for three years, and clear dead foliage and culls at season's end, since the sclerotia overwinter in them.
